title: De Gaudeif un sien Meester
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 68. Text from Wikisource (twice proofread against the original scans). 1857 spelling preserved exactly. This tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch); the glossary gives the High German equivalent for each dialect form.
about: KHM 68, told entirely in Low German (Plattdeutsch) like the fisherman’s tale and the juniper tree — the old speech of the north, so that nearly every word looks a little foreign beside the High German of the rest of the collection. A father goes into church to ask God what trade his son should learn, takes the sexton standing behind the altar for the voice of God, and apprentices the boy to a master thief; what the boy actually learns is shape-shifting, and the tale ends in a chase through animal forms that his master loses for good. Grimm prints his own glosses of the hardest dialect words in parentheses inside the text itself — those parentheses are his, not ours.

sentences.t: Jan wull sien Sohn en Handwerk lehren loeten, do gonk Jan in de Kerke un beddet to ussen Herrgott wat üm wull selig (zuträglich) wöre: do steit de Köster achter dat Altar un seg „dat Gaudeifen, dat Gaudeifen (gaudieben).“
sentences.l: Jan wanted to have his son learn a trade, so Jan went into the church and prayed to our Lord God what might be salutary for him: there stands the sexton behind the altar and says “thieving, thieving.”
sentences.i: Jan wanted his son to learn a trade, so he went into the church and prayed to our Lord God to know what would be best for him — and behind the altar stood the sexton, who said: “Thieving, thieving.”
sentences.n: This whole tale is in Low German (Plattdeutsch), the speech of the north, as KHM 19 and KHM 47 are. Here: wull = wollte in the first clause but wohl in the second (“wat üm wull selig wöre”), sien = sein, en = ein, loeten = lassen, do = da, gonk = ging, Kerke = Kirche, beddet = betete, ussen = unserem, wat = was, üm = ihm, wöre = wäre, steit = steht, achter = hinter, seg = sagt. Gaudeifen is the verb belonging to Gaudeif, High German Gaudieb, a sly thief or rogue — and Grimm glosses it himself in the 1857 text as “gaudieben”; every parenthesis in this tale is his. The sexton is hiding behind the altar and answering the prayer as though he were God.

sentences.t: Do geit Jan wier to sien Sohn, he möst dat Gaudeifen lehren, dat hedde em usse Herrgott segt.
sentences.l: Then Jan goes back to his son: he must learn the thieving, our Lord God had said that to him.
sentences.i: So Jan went back to his son: he was to learn thieving, for our Lord God had said so.
sentences.n: The tale slides freely between past and present — “wull” (wanted), then “geit” (goes) — as a spoken telling does, and it will keep doing so to the end. geit = geht, wier = wieder, möst = müsse, hedde = hätte, segt = gesagt.

sentences.t: Geit he met sienen Sohn un sögt sik enen Mann, de dat Gaudeifen kann.
sentences.l: He goes with his son and seeks himself a man who can do the thieving.
sentences.i: So off he went with his son to seek out a man who knew the thief’s trade.
sentences.n: The sentence starts straight in with its verb — “Geit he” — with no do or un in front of it; in a spoken tale this is a way of hurrying on. met = mit, sögt = sucht, sik = sich.

sentences.t: Do goht se ene ganze Tied, kummt in so’n graut Wold, do steit so’n klein Hüsken mot so’ne olle Frau derin; seg Jan „wiet ji nich enen Mann, de dat Gaudeifen kann?“
sentences.l: Then they walk a whole while, come into such a great wood; there stands such a little house with an old woman in it; says Jan “do you not know a man who can do the thieving?”
sentences.i: So they walked a long while and came into a great wood, and there stood a little house with an old woman inside; Jan said: “Do you not know of a man who knows the thief’s trade?”
sentences.n: goht = gehen, Tied = Zeit, graut = groß, Wold = Wald, mot = mit, olle = alte, derin = darin, “wiet ji” = wißt ihr. Hüsken is a diminutive in -ken where High German has -chen (Häuschen). ji is the plural “you” that strangers use to one another throughout this tale.

sentences.t: „Dat känn ji hier wull lehren,“ seg de Frau, „mien Sohn is en Meester dervon.“
sentences.l: “That you can well learn here,” says the woman, “my son is a master of it.”
sentences.i: “That you may well learn here,” said the woman; “my son is a master of it.”
sentences.n: känn ji = könnt ihr, mien = mein, dervon = davon.

sentences.t: Do kührt (spricht) he met den Sohn, of he dat Gaudeifen auk recht könne?
sentences.l: Then he speaks with the son, whether he can do the thieving properly too?
sentences.i: Then he spoke with the son, to ask whether he really knew the thief’s trade.
sentences.n: kühren is the Low German for “to speak” — Grimm supplies “(spricht)” in the text itself. of = ob, auk = auch. The question mark stands although the question is reported rather than quoted.

sentences.t: De Gaudeifsmeester seg „ick willt juen Sohn wull lehren, dann kummt övern Johr wier, wann ji dann juen Sohn noch kennt, dann will ick gar kien Lehrgeld hebben, un kenne ji em nig, dann müge ji mi twe hunnert Dahler giewen.“
sentences.l: The thief-master says “I will teach it to your son well enough; then come back a year from now. If you still know your son then, I will have no apprentice-money at all; and if you do not know him, then you must give me two hundred thalers.”
sentences.i: The master thief said: “I will teach your son well enough. Come back a year from now: if you still know your son then, I will take no apprentice-fee at all; but if you do not know him, you must give me two hundred thalers.”
sentences.n: “övern Johr” = übers Jahr, this time next year. Lehrgeld is the fee a father paid a master craftsman to take his boy on — the wager is over that fee. willt = will es, juen = euren, kien = kein, hebben = haben, nig = nicht, “twe hunnert Dahler” = zweihundert Taler.

sentences.t: De Vader geit wier noh Hues, un de Sohn lehret gut hexen un gaudeifen.
sentences.l: The father goes home again, and the son learns witchcraft and thieving well.
sentences.i: The father went home again, and the son learned witchcraft and thieving well.
sentences.n: lehren in this dialect does duty for both “teach” and “learn”: “de Sohn lehret” means the son learns. hexen = to work magic — the thief’s trade turns out to be shape-shifting.

sentences.t: Asse dat Johr um is, geit de Vader alle un grient wu he dat anfangen will, dat he sienen Sohn kennt.
sentences.l: When the year is up, the father goes off and weeps at how he shall set about it, that he may know his son.
sentences.i: When the year was up, off went the father, weeping and wondering how he should manage to know his son again.
sentences.n: Asse = als, “um is” = um ist, elapsed; grient = greint, weeps. “wu he dat anfangen will” = wie er das anfangen will, how he is to go about it. The small word alle here seems to mean something like “off, on his way”; its exact force in this Westphalian text is not certain, and we have left it light rather than choose a sense and sound sure of it.

sentences.t: Asse he der so geit un grient, do kümmt em so’n klein Männken in de Möte (entgegen), dat seg „Mann, wat grien ji? ji sind je so bedröft.“
sentences.l: As he walks along there weeping, a little manikin comes to meet him, and it says “man, what are you weeping for? you are so downcast.”
sentences.i: As he went along weeping, a little man came to meet him, and said: “Man, why do you weep? You are so downcast.”
sentences.n: “in de Möte kommen” = entgegenkommen, to come to meet — Grimm glosses it “(entgegen)” in the text. Männken = Männchen, and being a neuter diminutive it is picked up by dat, “it”, not “he”. der = da, bedröft = betrübt.

sentences.t: „O,“ seg Jan, „ick hebbe mienen Sohn vör en Johr bi en Gaudeifsmeester vermet, do sede de mig, ick söll övert Johr wier kummen, un wann ick dann mienen Sohn nich kennde, dann söll ick em twe hunnert Dahler giewen, un wann ick em kennde, dann höf ick nix to giewen; nu sin ick so bange dat ick em nig kenne, un ick weet nig, wo ick dat Geld her kriegen sall.“
sentences.l: “Oh,” says Jan, “a year ago I bound my son out to a thief-master; then he told me I should come back a year later, and if I did not know my son then, I should give him two hundred thalers, and if I did know him, I need give nothing; now I am so afraid that I shall not know him, and I do not know where I am to get the money from.”
sentences.i: “Oh,” said Jan, “a year ago I bound my son over to a master thief, and he told me to come back a year later; and if I did not know my son then, I was to give him two hundred thalers, but if I knew him I should owe nothing. Now I am so afraid I shall not know him, and I do not know where I am to find the money.”
sentences.n: vermet = vermietet, hired out — the word for putting a child into service. “höf ick nix to giewen” = ich brauchte nichts zu geben; höven is the Low German “to need”, and it survives in Dutch hoeven. “wo… her” = woher, from where. sede = sagte, söll = sollte, nix = nichts, weet = weiß, sall = soll.

sentences.t: Do seg dat Männken, he söll en Körsken Braut met niemen, un gohen unner den Komin stohen: „do up den Hahlbaum steit en Körfken, do kiekt en Vügelken uht, dat is jue Sohn.“
sentences.l: Then the manikin says he should take a crust of bread with him and go and stand under the chimney: “up there on the pot-beam stands a little basket, and a little bird looks out of it — that is your son.”
sentences.i: Then the little man said he should take a crust of bread with him and go and stand under the chimney: “Up there on the pot-beam stands a little basket, and a little bird looks out of it — that is your son.”
sentences.n: A Hahlbaum is the beam across an open hearth from which the pot-hook hangs, the smoke-blackened rafter of an old farmhouse kitchen. “Körsken Braut” = Krüstchen Brot, a crust of bread; Komin = Kamin; Körfken = Körbchen; Vügelken = Vögelchen; “kiekt uht” = guckt heraus; jue = euer.

sentences.t: Do geit Jan hen un schmit en Körsken Schwatbraut vör den Korf, do kümmt dat Vügelken daruht un blickt der up.
sentences.l: Then Jan goes there and throws a crust of black bread down before the basket; then the little bird comes out of it and looks at it.
sentences.i: So Jan went and threw a crust of black bread down before the basket, and the little bird came out and looked at it.
sentences.n: schmit = schmeißt, Schwatbraut = Schwarzbrot, daruht = da heraus, “blickt der up” = blickt darauf.

sentences.t: „Holla, mien Sohn, bist du hier?“ seg de Vader.
sentences.l: “Hullo, my son, are you here?” says the father.
sentences.n: Note the shift from the polite ji the father has used with strangers to du: he knows the bird is his own boy.

sentences.t: Do freude sick de Sohn dat he sienen Vader sog; awerst de Lehrmeester seg „dat het ju de Düvel in giewen, wu könn ji sus juen Sohn kennen?“
sentences.l: Then the son rejoiced that he saw his father; but the teaching-master says “the Devil has put that into you — how else could you know your son?”
sentences.i: Then the son rejoiced to see his father; but the master said: “The Devil has prompted you — how else could you have known your son?”
sentences.n: “ingiewen” = eingeben, to put a thing into someone’s mind, to prompt him; Düvel = Teufel. The master thief, whose own trade is witchcraft, complains that the other side has had supernatural help. sog = sah, awerst = aber, wu = wie, sus = sonst.

sentences.t: „Vader, loet us gohn“ sede de Junge.
sentences.l: “Father, let us go,” said the boy.

sentences.t: Do will de Vader met sienen Sohn nach Hues hengohn, unnerweges kümmt der ne Kutske an föhren, do segd de Sohn to sienen Vader „ick will mie in enen grauten Windhund maken, dann künn ji viel Geld met mie verdienen.“
sentences.l: Then the father wants to go home with his son; on the way a coach comes driving up, and the son says to his father “I will make myself into a great greyhound, then you can earn a lot of money with me.”
sentences.i: The father set off homewards with his son, and on the way a coach came driving up; then the son said to his father: “I will turn myself into a great greyhound, and you can make good money out of me.”
sentences.n: “sik in wat maken” = sich in etwas verwandeln, to turn oneself into something — the formula for every transformation in the rest of the tale. unnerweges = unterwegs, Kutske = Kutsche, “an föhren” = angefahren, mie = mich, “künn ji” = könnt ihr. Note “nach Hues” here where the tale writes “noh Hues” everywhere else: the 1857 printing is not consistent, and we keep what it prints.

sentences.t: Do röpt de Heer uht de Kutske „Mann, will ji den Hund verkaupen?“
sentences.l: Then the gentleman calls out of the coach “man, will you sell the dog?”
sentences.n: verkaupen = verkaufen. Low German kept the p that High German shifted to f and pf — hence up for auf, Kopp for Kopf, Perd for Pferd. Once you hear that one substitution, a great deal of this tale opens up.

sentences.t: „Jau,“ sede de Vader.
sentences.l: “Yes,” said the father.

sentences.t: „Wu viel Geld will ji den vör hebben?“
sentences.l: “How much money will you have for him?”

sentences.t: „Dertig Dahler.“
sentences.l: “Thirty thalers.”
sentences.n: Dertig = dreißig. A Thaler was a large silver coin; thirty of them is a serious price for a dog, and the buyer says so.

sentences.t: „Je, Mann, dat is je viel, men wegen dat et so’n eislicke rohren Ruen (gewaltig schöner Rüde) is, so will ick en behollen.“
sentences.l: “Well, man, that is a lot; but because it is such an uncommonly fine dog, I will keep him.”
sentences.i: “Well, man, that is a great deal; but seeing that he is such a mighty fine hound, I will take him.”
sentences.n: Grimm glosses “eislicke rohren Ruen” himself as “gewaltig schöner Rüde” — an awfully fine male dog; eislick is an intensifier of the same kind as English “awfully”, formed from a word for “dreadful”. men = aber, “wegen dat” = weil, behollen = behalten.

sentences.t: De Heer nimmt en in siene Kutske, asse de en lück (wenig) wegföhrt is, do sprinkt de Hund uht den Wagen dör de Glase, un do was he kien Windhund mehr un was wier bie sienen Vader.
sentences.l: The gentleman takes him into his coach; when he has driven a little way off, the dog springs out of the carriage through the glass, and then he was no greyhound any more and was back with his father.
sentences.i: The gentleman took him into his coach; and when he had driven a little way, the dog sprang out of the carriage through the glass — and he was a greyhound no longer, but back with his father.
sentences.n: lück = wenig, glossed by Grimm in the text. dör = durch; “de Glase” = die Gläser, the coach windows. The narration flips from present (“nimmt”, “sprinkt”) to past (“was”) inside a single sentence.

sentences.t: Do goht sie tosamen noh Hues.
sentences.l: Then they go home together.

sentences.t: Den annern Dag is in dat neigste Dorb Markt, do seg de Junge to sienen Vader „ick will mie nu in en schön Perd maken, dann verkaupet mie; awerst wann ji mie verkaupet, do möt ji mi den Taum uttrecken, süs kann ick kien Mensk wier weren.“
sentences.l: The next day there is a market in the nearest village, and the boy says to his father “now I will make myself into a fine horse; then sell me. But when you sell me, you must pull the bridle off me, or else I can never become a person again.”
sentences.i: The next day there was a market in the nearest village, and the boy said to his father: “Now I will turn myself into a fine horse; then sell me. But when you sell me, you must draw off the bridle, or else I can never be a man again.”
sentences.n: The bridle is the tale’s one rule, and the father is about to forget it. annern = anderen, neigste = nächste, Dorb = Dorf, Perd = Pferd, Taum = Zaum, uttrecken = ausziehen (separable ut-), süs = sonst, Mensk = Mensch, weren = werden.

sentences.t: Do treckt de Vader met dat Perd noh’t Markt, do kümmt de Gaudeifsmeester un köft dat Perd för hunnert Dahler, un de Vader verget un treckt em den Taum nig uht.
sentences.l: Then the father treks with the horse to the market; there comes the thief-master and buys the horse for a hundred thalers, and the father forgets and does not draw the bridle off him.
sentences.i: So the father went with the horse to the market; and the master thief came and bought the horse for a hundred thalers — and the father forgot, and did not draw off the bridle.
sentences.n: trecken means both “to pull” and “to go, to trek”: in one sentence the father treks to market and fails to pull the bridle off. And the buyer is the master thief himself, come to fetch his apprentice back. köft = kauft, verget = vergißt.

sentences.t: Do treckt de Mann met das Perd noh Hues, un doet et in en Stall.
sentences.l: Then the man treks home with the horse and puts it in a stable.
sentences.n: “met das Perd” — the High German das slips in where this tale writes dat everywhere else. doet = tut.

sentences.t: Asse de Magd öwer de Dehle geit, do segt dat Perd „tüh mie den Taum uht, tüh mie den Taum uht.“
sentences.l: When the maid goes across the house-floor, the horse says “pull the bridle off me, pull the bridle off me.”
sentences.i: When the maidservant went across the floor, the horse said: “Draw off my bridle, draw off my bridle.”
sentences.n: The Dehle (High German Diele) is the great earthen-floored hall of a North-German farmhouse — threshing floor, byre and through-passage at once, with the stalls opening off it. tüh = zieh.

sentences.t: Do steiht de Magd un lustert, „je, kannst du kühren?“
sentences.l: Then the maid stands and listens: “well, can you talk?”
sentences.i: Then the maid stopped and listened: “Why, can you speak?”
sentences.n: lustern = lauschen, to listen. kühren, “to speak”, is the word Grimm glossed near the start of the tale.

sentences.t: Geit hen un tüht em den Taum uht, do werd dat Perd en Lüning (Sperling), un flügt öwer de Döhre, un de Hexenmeester auk en Lüning, un flügt em noh.
sentences.l: She goes and pulls the bridle off him, and then the horse becomes a sparrow and flies out over the door, and the sorcerer too a sparrow, and flies after him.
sentences.i: She went and drew off the bridle, and the horse turned into a sparrow and flew out over the door; and the sorcerer became a sparrow too, and flew after him.
sentences.n: Lüning is Low German for a sparrow, and Grimm supplies “(Sperling)”. Döhre = Tür. The second half of the clause has no verb of its own — “un de Hexenmeester auk en Lüning” — the earlier werd is simply understood. Here the chase through shapes begins.

sentences.t: Do kümmt se bie ene (zusammen), un bietet sick, awerst de Meester verspielt un mäk sick in’t Water, un is en Fisk.
sentences.l: Then they come together and bite at each other, but the master loses and casts himself into the water and is a fish.
sentences.i: Then they came together and set on each other; but the master lost, and threw himself into the water and became a fish.
sentences.n: “bie ene kommen” = zusammenkommen, glossed by Grimm. verspielen is to lose at play — the contest of shapes is scored like a match. “mäk sick in’t Water”, literally “makes himself into the water”, is the same maken construction as every other transformation here.

sentences.t: Do werd de Junge auk en Fisk, un se bietet sick wier, dat de Meester verspielen mot.
sentences.l: Then the boy becomes a fish too, and they bite at each other again, so that the master must lose.

sentences.t: Do mäk sick de Meester in en Hohn, un de Junge werd en Voß un bitt den Meester den Kopp af; do is he storwen un liegt daut bes up düssen Dag.
sentences.l: Then the master makes himself into a hen, and the boy becomes a fox and bites the master’s head off; then he died and lies dead to this day.
sentences.i: Then the master turned himself into a hen, and the boy became a fox and bit the master’s head off; and so he died, and lies dead to this day.
sentences.n: “bitt den Meester den Kopp af” — the head is bitten off, and den Meester marks whose it is. storwen = gestorben, daut = tot, “bes up düssen Dag” = bis auf diesen Tag. The tale ends flat, with no wedding and no reward: the apprentice simply out-magics his master and kills him.
